editorial_reason: Read Stacks Set Theory 3.11, which recalls the covering-family axioms from Sites, Definition 7.6.2 and explicitly defines combinatorial equivalence of covering families. The section proves how to bound such covers, so I record the genuine categorical covering concept and its named equivalence.

definitions.text: For a site (C,Cov), a covering family of an object U is a collection of arrows {U_i→U} included in Cov(U), where the designated covering families contain isomorphism covers and are stable under compositional refinement and pullback along arrows into U.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: covering family in a Grothendieck site

definitions.text: Two families (f_i:U_i→U) and (g_j:V_j→U) are combinatorially equivalent when every map in either family occurs in the other, ignoring multiplicities and the indexing sets; equivalently each family admits an indexing map into the other identifying the arrows.
definitions.source_section: Section 3.11 paragraph before Lemma 3.11.1; Sites Definition 7.8.2
definitions.context_hint: Grothendieck sites: combinatorially equivalent covering families

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.165, specifically Lemma 10.165.1 and Definition 10.165.2. This establishes the geometric normality condition after arbitrary field extension, and its equivalent test using the perfect closure of the base field.

definitions.text: A k-algebra A is geometrically normal over a field k if for every extension of fields K/k the base-changed algebra K⊗_k A is a normal ring.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: geometrically normal algebra

definitions.text: Equivalently, a k-algebra A is geometrically normal if its scalar extension k^perf⊗_k A to the perfect closure of k is a normal ring; this also tests normality over all finite purely inseparable field extensions.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: alternative perfect-closure test for geometric normality

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.84 Definition 10.84.1 and Lemma 10.84.2. A transfinite filtration with split successor inclusions is a direct sum dévissage, and Kaplansky dévissage adds countable-generation of successor quotients.

definitions.text: A direct sum dévissage of an R-module M is an ordinal-indexed increasing family of submodules M_α starting at zero, continuous at limit ordinals and with union M, such that each successor inclusion M_α⊆M_{α+1} splits as a direct summand.
definitions.context_hint: Module theory: direct-sum transfinite dévissage

definitions.text: A Kaplansky dévissage of an R-module M is a direct sum dévissage whose every successive quotient M_{α+1}/M_α is a countably generated R-module.
definitions.context_hint: Module theory: Kaplansky transfinite dévissage

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.47 introductory definition of a geometrically irreducible algebra. This notion imposes irreducibility of the prime spectrum after every base-field extension and can be expressed as uniqueness of the minimal prime ideal.

definitions.text: A k-algebra A is geometrically irreducible over the field k when, for every field extension K/k, the ring A⊗_k K has exactly one minimal prime ideal, equivalently its prime spectrum is irreducible.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: geometrically irreducible k-algebra

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.75 introductory construction of Tor_i and Lemma 10.75.8. The derived tensor functors are defined through homology of a free resolution, and vanishing of Tor_1 with finitely generated ideal quotients is a correct equivalent flatness test.

definitions.text: For modules M and N over a commutative ring R and integer i≥0, Tor_i^R(M,N) is the ith homology module of F_•⊗_R N, where F_• is any free resolution of M; its isomorphism type is independent of that resolution.
definitions.context_hint: Homological algebra: derived tensor/Tor module

definitions.text: An R-module M is flat if and only if Tor_1^R(M,R/I)=0 for every finitely generated ideal I⊆R; equivalently, Tor_i^R(M,N)=0 for all R-modules N and every i>0.
definitions.context_hint: Homological algebra: Tor-vanishing criterion for module flatness

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 4.43 including Definitions 4.43.3, 4.43.5, 4.43.7, 4.43.8, 4.43.12 and 4.43.15. These specify mathematically distinct objects and structure-preserving maps; the symmetry condition must satisfy the coherence constraints.

definitions.text: A monoidal category consists of a category C, a bifunctor ⊗:C×C→C, a natural associativity isomorphism satisfying the pentagon, and a unit object 1 with natural unit isomorphisms satisfying the triangle coherence identity.
definitions.source_section: Definition 4.43.3; unit and associativity constraints in Section 4.43
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: monoidal category

definitions.text: A strong monoidal functor F:C→D between monoidal categories is a functor equipped with coherent natural isomorphisms F(X)⊗F(Y)≅F(X⊗Y) and a compatible identification of F(1_C) with the unit in D.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: strong monoidal functor

definitions.text: An object X in a monoidal category is tensor-invertible if there exists an object Y with X⊗Y≅1 and Y⊗X≅1, where 1 is the unit object.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: tensor-invertible monoidal object

definitions.text: A left dual Y of an object X in a monoidal category comes with maps η:1→X⊗Y and ε:Y⊗X→1 for which the resulting two triangle, or snake, composites on X and Y are the respective identity maps.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: left dual of a monoidal object

definitions.text: A symmetric monoidal category is a monoidal category equipped with a natural exchange isomorphism X⊗Y→Y⊗X that is involutive and compatible with the associator through the required coherence diagrams.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: symmetric monoidal category

definitions.text: A symmetric monoidal functor is a strong monoidal functor between symmetric monoidal categories whose structural tensor isomorphisms also commute with the symmetry/exchange isomorphisms of the two categories.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: symmetry-preserving strong monoidal functor

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 4.22 Definitions 4.22.1 and 4.22.2. The source explicitly gives different filtered (ind) and cofiltered (pro) notions, including a splitting through a stage and eventual compatibility equations; these are not simply the statement that a colimit or limit exists.

definitions.text: A filtered diagram M_i with cocone M_i→X is essentially constant with value X if some stage M_i admits a map X→M_i splitting M_i→X, and for every stage j the maps from M_j into a later common stage eventually agree with those factoring through X and the chosen M_i.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: essentially constant filtered diagram/ind-object

definitions.text: A cofiltered diagram M_i with cone X→M_i is essentially constant with value X if some stage M_i maps back to X splitting X→M_i, and for each stage j there exists a common earlier stage where the transition maps factor through X and the selected M_i.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: essentially constant inverse diagram/pro-object

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.16 Lemma 10.16.1. The named Cayley–Hamilton assertion is a theorem, but the section explicitly identifies the characteristic polynomial by a determinant construction; that is usable definitional content, unlike mistaking the theorem itself for a definition.

definitions.text: The characteristic polynomial of an n×n matrix A over a commutative ring R is the polynomial χ_A(t)=det(t I_n−A) in R[t], where I_n denotes the identity matrix.
definitions.context_hint: Linear algebra: characteristic polynomial of a square matrix

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.142 overview together with its cited Definition 10.137.1. Smooth ring homomorphisms are finite-presentation maps satisfying the projective-degree-zero naive cotangent complex condition, which is a precise definition and not just the overview's list of properties.

definitions.text: A homomorphism R→S of commutative rings is smooth when S is finitely presented as an R-algebra and the naive cotangent complex of S over R is quasi-isomorphic to a finite projective S-module concentrated in degree zero.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: smooth homomorphism of rings

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.127 on colimits and finite-presentation maps. It proves the filtered-colimit representation of R-algebras by finitely presented R-algebras (Lemma 10.127.1) and commuting properties of maps, but it does not introduce a new named mathematical object defined by the heading 'colimits and maps of finite presentation'.

Read Stacks 10.140, 'Smooth algebras over fields'. The section proves differential and regularity criteria for the already-defined notion of smoothness, including results under perfect or algebraically closed base fields; it does not add a separate definition specifically named by the section heading.

Read Stacks 4.5 Definition 4.5.1 defining a categorical coproduct of a pair by a universal mapping property, including the two structure inclusions and uniqueness of factorization toward arbitrary objects.

definitions.text: A coproduct of objects X,Y in a category C is an object P together with maps i:X→P and j:Y→P such that for any Z and arrows f:X→Z and g:Y→Z there is a unique h:P→Z satisfying h∘i=f and h∘j=g.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: binary coproduct of objects
